content.text:
Fixed. Changes are uncommitted, as asked.

## Root cause

`fetch` leaves two `abort` listeners on the signal you pass in:

- `lib/web/fetch/request.js:447` — the `Request` constructor makes its internal `AbortSignal` *follow* your signal by adding a listener to it. That listener was only ever removed on abort, or lazily by a `FinalizationRegistry` once the internal `AbortController` is garbage collected. Since GC is not prompt (and `fetching` now holds the request object alive for the duration of the request, per #4627), reusing one signal across many requests piles listeners up — hence the `9053 abort listeners added to [AbortSignal]` warning. The existing `setMaxListeners(1500, signal)` at `request.js:436` only pushed the threshold back.
- `lib/web/fetch/index.js:208` — the abort steps added in step 11 of the `fetch` method were never removed either (on a per-fetch internal signal, so not the warning source, but it retained the closure).

## Fix

- `request.js`: capture the disposer returned by `util.addAbortListener` and store a `#signalCleanup` closure that unregisters the finalizer and removes the listener; expose it via a private static accessor `cleanupRequestSignalListener` following the file's existing `getRequestState`/`getRequestDispatcher` pattern.
- `index.js`: `handleFetchDone` is now a per-fetch closure that calls both disposers before `finalizeAndReportTiming`. It runs as `processResponseEndOfBody`, i.e. after the response body is fully read/errored — by then `abortFetch` is a no-op anyway (the request body is consumed and the response stream is no longer readable), so nothing observable changes.

## Verification

With the cleanup temporarily disabled, 50 completed fetches sharing one signal left 50 `abort` listeners; with the fix, 0 — and aborting an in-flight request still rejects with `AbortError`.

New test `test/fetch/abort-signal-listener-cleanup.js` covers three completion paths (body read, body never read via a 204, and network error) plus the abort-still-works case. Also ran the existing fetch suite: 473 pass, 0 fail, including `long-lived-abort-controller.js` and `max-listeners.js`.

Fixed. Changes are uncommitted, as asked.

## Root cause

`fetch` leaves two `abort` listeners on the signal you pass in:

- `lib/web/fetch/request.js:447` — the `Request` constructor makes its internal `AbortSignal` *follow* your signal by adding a listener to it. That listener was only ever removed on abort, or lazily by a `FinalizationRegistry` once the internal `AbortController` is garbage collected. Since GC is not prompt (and `fetching` now holds the request object alive for the duration of the request, per #4627), reusing one signal across many requests piles listeners up — hence the `9053 abort listeners added to [AbortSignal]` warning. The existing `setMaxListeners(1500, signal)` at `request.js:436` only pushed the threshold back.
- `lib/web/fetch/index.js:208` — the abort steps added in step 11 of the `fetch` method were never removed either (on a per-fetch internal signal, so not the warning source, but it retained the closure).

## Fix

- `request.js`: capture the disposer returned by `util.addAbortListener` and store a `#signalCleanup` closure that unregisters the finalizer and removes the listener; expose it via a private static accessor `cleanupRequestSignalListener` following the file's existing `getRequestState`/`getRequestDispatcher` pattern.
- `index.js`: `handleFetchDone` is now a per-fetch closure that calls both disposers before `finalizeAndReportTiming`. It runs as `processResponseEndOfBody`, i.e. after the response body is fully read/errored — by then `abortFetch` is a no-op anyway (the request body is consumed and the response stream is no longer readable), so nothing observable changes.

## Verification

With the cleanup temporarily disabled, 50 completed fetches sharing one signal left 50 `abort` listeners; with the fix, 0 — and aborting an in-flight request still rejects with `AbortError`.

New test `test/fetch/abort-signal-listener-cleanup.js` covers three completion paths (body read, body never read via a 204, and network error) plus the abort-still-works case. Also ran the existing fetch suite: 473 pass, 0 fail, including `long-lived-abort-controller.js` and `max-listeners.js`.

One thing I did not change: if a response's body is neither read nor errored, `processResponseEndOfBody` never fires and the listener still waits on GC. That path also leaks the socket, so it's a pre-existing and separate issue.
